newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Apple can't afford to cut licensing - cloner.
newsitem.headline: Apple can't afford to cut licensing - cloner.

text.p: A major clone maker of Apple Computer said on Wednesday the embattled U.S. company would be "committing a suicide" if it decided to curb or end licensing agreements with makers of Macintosh clones.

Taiwan's Umax Data Systems, which has a contract to make Macintosh operating systems until the end of 1998, said its chairman would discuss the issue with Apple's co-founder Steve Jobs at the Macworld trade show now taking place in Boston.
"Our chairman Frank Huang will meet with Steve Jobs in the next day or so to find out what's going on," an Umax spokeswoman said in Taipei.
"We don't think Apple can honestly stop selling its licences, because that would be committing a suicide for Apple's products," she said.

Apple, which began licensing Mac technology a few years ago, is having a testy relationship with cloners. Some executives are regretting the decision because clone makers have cut into the firm's sales by selling products at cheaper prices.
Huang had said in an earlier interview with Reuters that his company has helped keep Apple alive even though it took away some of its business.
"If it weren't for the clone makers to promote its products, Apple would be even worse off right now," Huang said.
"Several years ago Apple absolutely hated the idea of clones, but now it absolutely depends on clones," he said.
Analysts have said the Macintosh operating system's share of the market has increased in recent months because of the success of the clone makers.
Another Macintosh cloner, Power Computing Corp, has criticised Apple for dragging out software licensing negotiations and named Jobs, who now serves as a strategic adviser, as the culprit.
"It appears at this point that Steve's attitude toward licensing is permeating throughout the organisation," Power Computing chairman Joel Kocker said on Tuesday at Macworld.
For the past two years Apple has been scrambling to devise improvements to the Macintosh that would set it apart from PCs.
Until 1995, Apple had relied on its computers' famed ease-of-use as a selling point, but Microsoft's release of Windows 95 took away much of the impact.
